description: Hi! I'm Elson, a Computer Science student majoring in Cybersecurity at Swinburne Sarawak. I'm interested in web development, problem-solving, and space technology. For Martian Map, I hope to help build an interactive map using NASA's Mars data. I'm looking for enthusiastic teammates with skills in programming, UI/UX, data analysis, GIS/3D mapping, or astronomy. Most importantly, let's collaborate, learn, and create something innovative together! 🚀
summary:
Picture stepping out of a Mars habitat with 8 hours of air on your back and no map made for walking. Mars has been studied for decades, but the data is spread across many missions and shown at a zoomed-out scale. That's no use to an astronout on foot. 
MarsWay is our answer: think of a Google Maps for walking on Mars, with a safety officer built in. We're a team of 6 university students from Sarawak, and we built around a future crewed walk at Gale Crater, near the boxwork ridges Curiosity explored in 2025. MarsWay ground temperature, and Curiosity's radiation and wheather readings. 
The day before a walk, the crew plan the easiest route between science stops. They see walking times for a suited astronout, a directions, a turn-back timer and solar or dust storm alerts with a route to shelter. 
It all comes down to one question: can we get there, and back, safely ?
details:
MarsWay

What does MarsWay do, and how does it work?

MarsWay is a planning and navigation app for astronauts walking on Mars. We like to call it "Google Maps for walking on Mars, with a safety officer built in." It works in two stages, like a real field trip.

  • The day before, in the habitat (Planning screen): the crew opens a close-up 3 km map of Gale Crater, near the boxwork ridges Curiosity explored in 2025. They can switch layers on and off: high-resolution photos, slope, ground temperature, minerals and Curiosity's actual track. MarsWay plans the easiest walking route between science stops and gives walking times for someone in a heavy suit. It also estimates the radiation dose and shows a coloured "safe to go" zone: green means the crew can go there and still get home, amber means only by using their reserve air, and outside the zone they can't. Every stop has a real Curiosity photo, so the crew knows what the ground will look like. The schedule can be downloaded as a CSV file for mission control.
  • During the walk (Walk screen on an Android phone): the screen shows the direction and distance to the next stop and a turn-back timer that counts down to the latest moment the crew can safely head home. It also gives a GO / NO-GO answer on whether there's time for a bonus stop.
  • Mars doesn't always go to plan, so MarsWay also simulates random events: local dust storms that slow walking, dust devils the crew has to wait out, solar storms that double radiation (with a route to shelter), rover breakdowns, and planet-wide dust storms that cancel the walk. Each scenario has a number, so the Planning and Walk screens show the same events and a mission can be replayed.

We built six walks (EVA-07 to EVA-12), including the Boxwork Walk and a trip toward the Gediz Vallis channel. Each walk has an on-foot version and a with-rover version.

What benefits does it have?

  • One map instead of ten. Data from HiRISE, CTX, MOLA, THEMIS, CRISM, Curiosity's RAD and REMS instruments, and NASA DONKI comes together in one place.
  • Clear answers, not raw data. Instead of reading slope maps, the crew sees "GO, 20 min to spare" or "Turn back now."
  • Safety by default. The app always works out the way home, not just the way out.
  • Works without internet. It runs fully in the browser with no server. The phone loads one small, ready-made file (about 0.7 MB), which matters on a planet with no signal towers.

What is the intended impact?

We want to show how decades of NASA Mars data can become a practical tool for the first people who walk there. The same idea could help mission planners today, Earth teams in remote areas such as deserts and polar regions, and students learning how real missions balance science against safety.

What tools did we use?

  • Data processing: Python, GDAL, rasterio, NumPy and QGIS, used to cut out our area, work out slope and roughness from the HiRISE 3D height map, and export map layers
  • Route finding: A* search with Tobler's hiking function, adjusted for a spacesuit
  • Safe zone: a Dijkstra search outward from the habitat, giving the walk-home time from every 5 m square
  • App: JavaScript, Vite, Leaflet for the maps and Three.js for the 3D view
  • Phone app: Capacitor, which wraps the web app as an Android app
  • Teamwork: GitHub (pull requests and automated tests) and Google Drive for the large NASA files

How is MarsWay creative?

Most Mars maps are made for scientists looking down from orbit. We turned the view around and asked what an astronaut on foot needs. That led to features you won't find in normal map tools: a safe zone that shrinks as the suit's air runs down, a turn-back timer, and storms that change the plan halfway through a walk. Every stop is at a real place Curiosity visited, with a real photo, so the mission is fictional but built on real ground.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Suit limits: 8 hours of suit time with a 2-hour reserve that the plan never uses
  • Terrain: a warning above 15° slope, no-go above 25°, and avoiding rough, rocky ground
  • Radiation: Curiosity's measured dose rate, doubled during solar storms, with a running total against NASA's 600 mSv career limit
  • Weather: walking slows to 0.6× speed in a dust storm
  • Rover use: drive time counts against suit time, and every rover walk has a walk-back plan in case the rover breaks down
  • Honesty: where we had to estimate (walking speed, storm odds), we say so in the app and keep the numbers in one place so they're easy to change
  • Ease of use: a tired astronaut in gloves needs big, simple messages, so the Walk screen shows only what matters right now
